title: Computer Networks
description: OSI model, TCP/IP, protocols and networking concepts for GATE, UGC NET and campus placements.

cards.question: List the 7 layers of the OSI model from top to bottom.
cards.answer: Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical.

cards.question: What is the difference between TCP and UDP?
cards.answer: TCP: connection-oriented, reliable, ordered, flow control. UDP: connectionless, faster, no guarantees — used for video, DNS, gaming.

cards.question: What is the three-way handshake?
cards.answer: TCP connection setup: (1) SYN from client (2) SYN-ACK from server (3) ACK from client. Establishes sequence numbers.

cards.question: What is the purpose of the IP address?
cards.answer: Uniquely identifies a device on a network at the Network layer, enabling routing of packets across networks.

cards.question: What is the difference between IPv4 and IPv6?
cards.answer: IPv4: 32-bit, ~4.3 billion addresses. IPv6: 128-bit, ~3.4×10³⁸ addresses, also adds built-in security and no NAT needed.

cards.question: What is CIDR notation?
cards.answer: Classless Inter-Domain Routing: IP address written as X.X.X.X/n where n is the number of bits in the network prefix. e.g. 192.168.1.0/24.

cards.question: What is the purpose of DNS?
cards.answer: Domain Name System: translates human-readable domain names (google.com) to IP addresses.

cards.question: What is the difference between HTTP and HTTPS?
cards.answer: HTTPS adds TLS/SSL encryption over HTTP, ensuring confidentiality, integrity and server authentication.

cards.question: What is ARP?
cards.answer: Address Resolution Protocol: maps an IP address to a MAC (hardware) address on a local network.

cards.question: What is the difference between a hub, switch and router?
cards.answer: Hub: broadcasts to all ports (Physical layer). Switch: forwards to the specific port (Data Link). Router: routes between networks (Network layer).

cards.question: What is NAT?
cards.answer: Network Address Translation: allows multiple devices on a private network to share a single public IP address by translating port numbers.

cards.question: What is flow control in TCP?
cards.answer: Uses a sliding window mechanism. The receiver advertises a window size; the sender can only have that many unacknowledged bytes in flight at once.

cards.question: What is congestion control in TCP?
cards.answer: Prevents too much data from overwhelming the network. Key algorithms: slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit, fast recovery.

cards.question: What is subnetting?
cards.answer: Dividing a larger network into smaller sub-networks by borrowing bits from the host portion of an IP address, reducing broadcast domains.

cards.question: What port numbers do HTTP, HTTPS, FTP and SSH use by default?
cards.answer: HTTP: 80, HTTPS: 443, FTP: 21 (control) / 20 (data), SSH: 22.

cards.question: What is the difference between a MAC address and an IP address?
cards.answer: MAC: hardware address burned in the NIC, used within a LAN (Data Link layer). IP: logical address assigned by network admin, used for routing across networks (Network layer).

cards.question: What is DHCP?
cards.answer: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol: automatically assigns IP addresses, subnet masks, gateways and DNS servers to devices on a network.

cards.question: What is the difference between connection-oriented and connectionless services?
cards.answer: Connection-oriented (TCP): establishes a connection first, guarantees delivery and order. Connectionless (UDP): sends packets independently, no setup, no guarantee.

cards.question: What is ICMP and what is it used for?
cards.answer: Internet Control Message Protocol: used for error reporting and diagnostics. Powers the `ping` and `traceroute` commands.

cards.question: What is a CDN?
cards.answer: Content Delivery Network: a geographically distributed set of servers that cache content close to users, reducing latency and load on origin servers.
